keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. Infobox "Dates: c. 5400-4500 BC"; Vinča A 5400/5300-5200, B 5200-5000/4950, C 5000/4950-4850/4800, D 4850/4800-4600/4500 BC; Chapman (1981) dates the culture "between 5700 and 4200 BC". Whole Serbia and Kosovo plus the named Hungarian, Romanian and north-west Bulgarian units; Montenegro is listed but not drawn (no site named). The Danube, Morava and Tisza are not mentioned on the page. No area figure to compare.

ledger.note: 5400 BCE: the Vinča culture, with its tells, copper mines and signs, succeeds the Starcevo on the Danube and Morava. Infobox "c. 5400-4500 BC", "Preceded by: Starčevo culture"; Vinča A "5400/5300-5200 BC"; "Copper ores were mined on a large scale at sites like Rudna Glava".
4850 BCE: the Late Vinča period (Vinča D, "4850/4800-4600/4500 BC") begins.

region.text: "corresponding mainly to modern-day Serbia and Kosovo, but also parts of Southernmost Hungary, Western-Central Romania", with Bulgaria, North Macedonia, Bosnia and Montenegro also listed; Vinča-Belo Brdo, Pločnik, Rudna Glava, Gomolava

ledger.note: 4500 BCE: the Vinča network dissolves. "Eventually the network lost its cohesion altogether and fell into decline", with declining soil fertility "after two millennia of intensive farming" partly to blame; infobox "Followed by: Tiszapolgár culture", which no dossier draws, so the land goes to nobody.

certainty.note: An archaeological culture drawn by modern units and radii, never a frontier.

sources.title: Vinča culture
sources.note: Dates and sub-phases, the countries covered, the type site and the mines, the decline.

notes: Culture dossier, one page. Overlap: the Starcevo dossier hands the Serbian core over in 5400 BCE; the Koros plain (Csongrad) passes to the Alföld LBK in 5300 BCE and is also drawn here as "Southernmost Hungary". The Tiszapolgár culture (from c. 4500 BC) that follows has no dossier (gap). Gazetteer: Vinča-Belo Brdo, Pločnik, Rudna Glava, Gomolava are not places; "Serbia" resolves as a country alias of "Republic of Serbia".
